claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is presented as a high-temperature, single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloy in a disordered solid-solution state.
Refractory bcc high-entropy alloys can have a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range order.
Above 1000 K, the target alloy remains single-phase bcc while SRO clustering is thermodynamically favorable and phase separation is suppressed.
Standard interatomic potentials may fail to predict SRO evolution accurately in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Controlled thermal aging or rapid quenching can tune the amount and connectivity of SRO in the target alloy.
SRO clusters can grow into a connected, percolating network without forming a secondary phase.
A percolating SRO network alters the distribution of phonon mean free paths.
At low SRO volume fractions, increased phonon scattering reduces thermal conductivity.
As SRO clusters grow, they form coherent regions with less mass-fluctuation scattering than the disordered matrix.
Connected coherent SRO regions act as low-scattering thermal pathways that increase thermal conductivity after percolation.
The conductivity transition is controlled by SRO-network connectivity rather than by additive scattering from independent clusters.
Thermal conductivity has a minimum at a critical SRO volume fraction and then rises when the SRO network percolates.
Serial, parallel, rule-of-mixtures, and effective-medium models predict a monotonic conductivity decrease with increasing SRO because they omit percolative connectivity.
The proposed percolative transition is limited to single-phase bcc alloys and is unlikely in fcc or multiphase alloys.
The potential-energy surface must accurately reproduce the energetic driving forces for clustering and SRO evolution.
The predicted percolation threshold and conductivity increase depend on the chosen interatomic potential.
Atomic-scale SRO connectivity is experimentally difficult to quantify.
Changes in diffuse-scattering intensity and correlation length from high-temperature X-ray diffraction and neutron scattering can identify SRO percolation.
A conductivity increase coincident with detected SRO percolation supports the hypothesis, whereas continued monotonic decrease with increasing SRO falsifies it.
